blocks.text: FC 27 Streamlined SBCs – Teardown and Redesign

blocks.html:
When cards become points, the points table becomes the economy. FC 27's Streamlined SBCs swap the squad-building puzzle for a score bar, and players like it: EA reported a positive reception within a week. But the change moved every important decision into one table, the Item Score curve, and that table has two problems.

1. Value. The curve jumps at ratings 81 and 84, while 82–84 cards cost about the same. One rating becomes the obvious fodder, and the 76–83 cards that fill most clubs barely move the bar.

2. Safety. The score bar makes submitting fast and irreversible, with no way to protect a card. In launch week a list bug let one player submit a 3-million-coin ICON by mistake, and a way to protect cards is now a widely requested fix.

Proposals: an even 28% step per rating from 75 to 84, keeping 84 and above unchanged; tested first as a limited-time event before any permanent change. Plus a quick win: a "protected" flag and a warning when one card would cover most of a target.

Evidence level: mechanics from EA's official notes and developer update; Item Scores and launch-week prices measured by the community from the live game, because EA doesn't publish them; my own play log in progress.

Squad Building Challenges (SBCs) are Ultimate Team's main sink: players give up cards in exchange for packs or special players. In FC 27, routine SBCs became "Streamlined": each card adds its Item Score to a bar, and the reward unlocks when the bar reaches the target.

blocks.caption: [Traditional] Streamlined SBCs swap a Squad Puzzle for a Score Bar

blocks.html: The whole system now rests on one table: how many points each card is worth. In the community-measured table, bronzes are worth 20, silvers 35, and gold cards from 90 (rated 75) to 14,000 (rated 90). Special versions such as Team of the Week score more than base cards of the same rating.
EA's stated goal for FC 27 is to "reduce repetitive friction" while keeping "meaningful decisions". For routine rewards, the Streamlined format delivers on the first half well.

blocks.html:
The split is the smartest part: routine rewards become quick, and puzzle SBCs stay as optional content for the players who like them. The design's success therefore depends on one number: how much each card is worth. That is the Item Score curve.

It's working with players, too. EA's 1 October developer update calls the reception positive, and Streamlined SBCs were added to the Companion App on 28 September. That's why this teardown proposes tuning, not a redesign.
Below 85, the Item Score curve is not smooth. Most ratings are worth 11–21% more than the one below, but 81 is worth 56% more and 84 is worth 102% more.

blocks.title: Two jumps, at 81 and 84, break an otherwise even gold curve
blocks.note: Each rating's Item Score as a percentage increase on the rating below. Community-measured in launch week; 85 and above are unchanged by the proposal.

blocks.html: The jumps matter because the market doesn't follow them. In launch week, 82s, 83s and 84s all sold at about the same price, the quick-sell floor of 600–650 coins. Score per coin therefore jumped with the curve:

blocks.html:
Two things follow from this.

1. One rating becomes the answer. For any SBC you can't fill from your club, buying 84s is more than twice as efficient as 82s. The "meaningful decision" EA wanted collapses into one rule, the one fodder guides were already publishing in launch week.

2. Most of a club is worth very little. An 84 is worth about four and a half 80s, or 41 bronzes. A 75,000-point SBC would take 91 84s or 417 80s. Cards rated 76–83 add little per card, which works against reducing friction for players whose clubs are mostly made of them.

The market may partly correct the first problem by pushing 84 prices up over time. It can't fix the second: a card's SBC value is set by the table, not by its price.

A player's view

Picture a player opening a 20,000-point SBC with 45 spare golds. Today, the 5 cards rated 84 do more than a third of the work, and the other 40 cards together add less than twice as much.

With the proposal, the same club covers three quarters of the target, and the player needs to buy 7 cards instead of 11 to finish. The club they built up through play is what changes, not the price of anything.

What the current curve gets right

A teardown should argue the other side first. EA hasn't explained the curve, so these are my inferences about what it's protecting:

blocks.html: The second goal matters more this year. EA's October developer update says coin balances are over 50% higher than at the same point last year, so any change that adds value to the economy has to be paid for somewhere. That's why the proposal is anchored and paired with target retuning, rather than a straight buff.

The score table doesn't only decide SBCs. Packs fill clubs with cards, players choose what to do with each card, and SBCs turn cards back into packs. Changing what a card is worth for SBCs touches every step.

blocks.text: Proposal: An Even Step from 75 to 84

blocks.html:
Keep 75 at 90 points and 84 at 830, and fill the ratings between with the same 28% step each time. Ratings 85 and above stay exactly as they are.


score(r) = 90 * 1.28r-75               75<= r <=84


That gives 75 = 90, 76 = 115, 77 = 147, 78 = 189, 79 = 242, 80 = 309, 81 = 396, 82 = 507, 83 = 648, 84 = 830.

rows: 80-rated cards needed for a 20,000 SBC
83-rated cards needed for a 20,000 SBC
84-rated cards needed for a 20,000 SBC
Cost per point, 82 vs 84 (launch-week prices)
SBC targets that need retuning
Only SBCs whose fodder is mostly rated 75–83

blocks.html:
Why This Shape

• Anchored at 84. Every SBC filled with 84s or better needs exactly the same cards as today, so the high-end economy and its reward values don't move.

• No breakpoint. Each rating is worth the same step more than the one below, so no single rating becomes "the" answer. Players can use whatever 76–83s they already own.

• One change, patch-sized. It is a table edit, not a new system. It can ship mid-season and be rolled back.

Alternatives I Considered

• Raise quick-sell values so prices follow score. Rejected: quick-sell creates coins, so this would inflate the whole coin economy, not just SBCs.

• A bonus for untradeable cards. Interesting for "use your club", but it adds a rule to a system whose point is having fewer rules.

• Smooth the whole curve, including 85+. Rejected for now: it would change the value of high-rated cards that players have already stockpiled and paid for.

The score bar made submitting faster and more frequent, but the safety rails didn't grow with it.

  • Submissions can't be undone. Submitted cards leave the club immediately, and EA's position is that "SBC submissions are final" and advisors can't restore them.
  • The old format had a built-in check. Building a squad meant looking at every card. Streamlined SBCs remove that step on purpose, so mistakes are cheaper to make.
  • It has already gone wrong. On 28 September a list display bug showed a 48-rated bronze while submitting a 90-rated ICON worth about 3 million coins. The only visible clue was the Item Score: 21,000 instead of 20.
  • Players are building their own workaround. Community guides now tell players to park valuable cards in Evolutions, because that blocks them from SBCs. Players have asked EA for a proper way to mark cards.

Quick win (no economy impact)
1. A "protected" flag on any card, which keeps it out of every SBC list until removed.
2. A warning when one card would cover more than half of a target, or when a card is a special version such as an ICON. One extra tap, shown only when the stakes are high.

The principle: when you make an action faster and more frequent, its safety checks have to scale with it. This fix also saves support time, since lost cards can't be restored.

blocks.text: Risks and how to Measure Success

blocks.html: The biggest risk is the Gallery: it uses the same Item Score, so this change would also make Gallery sets easier to grade.

blocks.html: I don't have EA's baseline numbers, so these are directions rather than exact thresholds. A team with telemetry would set the thresholds from the current values.

Don't change the table straight away. Run the proposal as a one-week live event first, using tools a live-ops team already has.

1. "Club Clear-out" week. A set of event SBCs where cards rated 76–83 score at the proposed values. Everything else, including the Gallery, stays on the current table, so the biggest risk is contained.

2. Compare with a normal week of similar SBCs: share of score from one rating, share of cards that were already in the club, completion rate, and coins spent on fodder.

3. Decide. Make it permanent if players use more of their own clubs without completion rates jumping, which would mean too many rewards entering the game. If completions jump, keep the curve but raise those SBCs' targets.

The event also works as content in its own right: a reason to open old cards, and a week players can look forward to.
